note: Hand-written equipment notes for the Ukraine page. Each entry names its side, speciality, an as-of date and a source. The importer adds Wikidata ids, articles and licensed images. Numbers are public estimates and say whose. An entry sets "image": false when the closest Wikidata match is a generic concept whose picture would misrepresent this war.

items.name: Orlan-10
items.role: Tactical reconnaissance and artillery spotting drone
items.description: Russia's workhorse reconnaissance drone since 2014: a catapult-launched, petrol-engined aircraft flying for many hours with a camera turret, used to find targets for artillery and to relay corrections. Cheap enough to lose in numbers, and lost in numbers; its imported electronics have appeared in sanctions reporting.
items.numbers: Oryx has documented well over a thousand Orlan-10 and Orlan-30 losses since 2022 (visually confirmed, an undercount by design).

items.name: ZALA 421-16E
items.role: Reconnaissance drone from the Lancet's maker
items.description: A flying-wing reconnaissance drone from the ZALA Aero group of Kalashnikov Concern, normally paired with Lancet loitering munitions: the ZALA finds the target and the Lancet strikes it. Its long endurance and quiet electric motor make it hard to spot from the ground.

items.name: Supercam S350
items.role: Medium reconnaissance drone
items.description: A series of catapult-launched reconnaissance drones built by Unmanned Systems Group in Izhevsk, flown for artillery reconnaissance and for cueing strikes behind the line. Reported to be one of the more common Russian types seen over Ukrainian positions from 2023.

items.name: Leleka-100
items.role: Reconnaissance drone in Ukrainian service
items.description: A Ukrainian-built electric reconnaissance drone from DeViRo, adopted by the armed forces in 2021 and produced in growing numbers since. It spots for artillery and drone strikes and is one of several domestic types, with Shark and Furia, that replaced imported quadcopters for deeper reconnaissance.

items.name: Shark
items.role: Reconnaissance drone for HIMARS and artillery targeting
items.description: Ukrspecsystems' Shark reconnaissance drone entered service in 2022 and is often cited with long-range strikes, spotting for HIMARS and guided artillery at ranges of tens of kilometres. Ukraine has produced later variants with better resistance to jamming.

items.name: FPV strike drones (Russia)
items.role: First-person-view quadcopters carrying a warhead
items.description: Cheap racing-style quadcopters flown through goggles into vehicles, positions and individual soldiers, now the main killer on the front line for both sides. Russia scaled production through 2023 and 2024 with volunteer workshops and state-backed factories, and both sides count monthly deliveries in the hundreds of thousands.
items.numbers: Both governments have stated production plans in the millions per year; no independent count exists.

items.name: FPV strike drones (Ukraine)
items.role: First-person-view quadcopters carrying a warhead
items.description: Ukraine's FPV programme grew from volunteer builds in 2022 to hundreds of manufacturers and a dedicated Unmanned Systems Forces branch in 2024. FPVs with RPG warheads or shaped charges account for a large share of reported Russian vehicle losses, and strike units publish confirmed hits through a points-based system.
items.numbers: Ukraine's government stated a goal of several million FPV drones for 2025; no independent count exists.

items.name: Fibre-optic FPV drones (Russia)
items.role: Jam-proof FPV controlled through a spooled fibre
items.description: From late 2024 Russia fielded FPV drones controlled through a thin optical fibre unspooled in flight, immune to radio jamming and able to fly into cellars and treelines. They were prominent in the Kursk fighting and along the Pokrovsk axis, at the cost of shorter range and fibres snagging on terrain.

items.name: Fibre-optic FPV drones (Ukraine)
items.role: Jam-proof FPV controlled through a spooled fibre
items.description: Ukraine followed Russia's fibre-optic drones within months, with domestic spools of 10 to 20 kilometres and longer announced during 2025. Units use them where electronic warfare is dense, accepting the weight of the spool for a link that cannot be jammed.

items.name: ZALA Lancet
items.role: Loitering munition against artillery, air defence and armour
items.description: A tube-shaped loitering munition with cruciform wings that dives onto a target seen through its own camera, often cued by a ZALA reconnaissance drone. From 2023 it became Russia's most effective weapon against Ukrainian howitzers and air defence radars behind the line, and later versions added automatic target recognition.
items.numbers: Open-source trackers count thousands of published Lancet strike videos; the share that hit is disputed.

items.name: ZALA KUB
items.role: Flying-wing loitering munition
items.description: A small flying-wing loitering munition from the same maker as the Lancet, used from the first weeks of the invasion against fixed positions. It lacks the Lancet's precision against moving targets and appears less often in strike footage.

items.name: Switchblade 300 and 600
items.role: US loitering munitions supplied in aid packages
items.description: The Switchblade 300 is a small, short-range munition against infantry; the 600 carries an anti-armour warhead over longer range. Supplied from 2022, they mattered early but were overtaken by Ukraine's cheaper domestic FPV drones, which are produced in far greater numbers.
items.numbers: US aid announcements listed several hundred Switchblade 300s in 2022 and later Switchblade 600s.

items.name: Shahed-136 / Geran-2
items.role: Long-range one-way attack drone against cities and energy
items.description: A delta-wing drone with a petrol engine and a warhead of around 50 kilograms, first used by Russia in September 2022 and built since 2023 at Alabuga in Tatarstan as the Geran-2. Launched in waves of hundreds with decoys to saturate air defence, it is the main weapon of the strike campaign against Ukrainian cities and the power grid. Later versions add jet engines, larger warheads and jam-resistant navigation.
items.numbers: Ukraine's Air Force reported record nights of over 700 drones and decoys in 2025; the General Staff's cumulative drone claim is shown in the figures above.

items.name: Geran-3 (jet Shahed)
items.role: Jet-powered one-way attack drone
items.description: A jet-engined development of the Shahed family, faster and harder for mobile fire groups to catch, used in growing numbers from 2025 inside the larger propeller-driven waves. Its speed cuts the time air defence has to react.

items.name: An-196 Liutyi
items.role: Long-range one-way attack drone against Russian refineries and airfields
items.description: A Ukrainian-built one-way attack drone with a range reported at around 1,000 kilometres, credited with many of the strikes on Russian oil refineries, depots and airfields from 2024. It sits at the heavy end of a family of Ukrainian long-range drones that also includes the Bober and UJ-22.

items.name: FP-1
items.role: Mass-produced long-range attack drone
items.description: A cheaper long-range attack drone from the Ukrainian firm Fire Point, shown publicly in 2025 with a stated production rate of over a hundred a day and a range of several hundred kilometres. It gives Ukraine a Shahed-like weapon for the campaign against Russian energy and logistics.
items.numbers: Fire Point stated production of around 100 a day in 2025; unverified.

items.name: Palianytsia and Peklo
items.role: Jet-powered drone-missiles
items.description: Ukraine's jet-powered 'missile-drones', announced in 2024, sit between a cruise missile and an attack drone: cheaper than a missile, faster than a Shahed. Palianytsia and the later Peklo were presented as strike weapons against airfields and depots within several hundred kilometres.

items.name: Interceptor drones (Ukraine)
items.role: Cheap drones that ram Shaheds and reconnaissance drones
items.description: Fast quadcopters and fixed-wing interceptors built to fly into Shahed drones, Orlans and Zalas at a fraction of the cost of a missile. Ukraine announced large purchases and production targets in 2025 as Shahed waves grew, with claims of hundreds of interceptions a night on the busiest nights.
items.numbers: Ukraine stated goals of 1,000 interceptor drones a day in 2025; unverified.

items.name: Interceptor drones (Russia)
items.role: Drones that hunt Ukrainian reconnaissance and long-range drones
items.description: Russia has fielded its own interceptor drones against Ukrainian reconnaissance types and the long-range drones flying at its refineries, alongside conventional air defence and helicopters used as drone hunters.

items.name: MAGURA V5
items.role: Uncrewed surface vessel that drove the Black Sea Fleet from Sevastopol
items.description: A Ukrainian naval drone from Defence Intelligence's programme, credited with sinking or damaging Russian warships and landing craft in 2023 and 2024 and, fitted with air-to-air missiles, with shooting down helicopters and even jets in 2025. Together with the Sea Baby it made Sevastopol unsafe for the fleet.

items.name: Sea Baby
items.role: Security Service naval drone used against the Crimean Bridge
items.description: The SBU's naval drone, used in the July 2023 attack on the Crimean Bridge and against ships and ports. Later versions carried rocket launchers and launched FPV drones from the sea.

items.name: Ground robots (Ukraine)
items.role: Tracked and wheeled robots for logistics, mining and casualty evacuation
items.description: From 2024 Ukraine issued growing numbers of small ground robots that carry supplies, lay mines and evacuate the wounded along drone-watched routes where a human on foot is likely to be hit. Some carry machine guns or explosive charges.

items.name: Starlink
items.role: Satellite internet that carries Ukrainian battlefield communications
items.description: SpaceX's low-orbit constellation has carried much of Ukraine's tactical communications, drone video and command traffic since 2022, with tens of thousands of terminals paid for by allies. Its availability has been a political question, and Russia has obtained terminals through third countries despite restrictions.
items.numbers: Ukraine reported over 40,000 terminals in use by 2024.

items.name: Starlink (illicit Russian use)
items.role: Terminals bought abroad and used by Russian units
items.description: Ukrainian intelligence and journalists reported from 2024 that Russian units were using Starlink terminals bought through intermediaries, giving them the same fast links for drone control. SpaceX said it does not sell to Russia and has disabled terminals it identifies.

items.name: R-187P1 Azart
items.role: Russian encrypted tactical radio
items.description: Russia's main modern handheld tactical radio, meant to give encrypted frequency-hopping links to small units. Its patchy issue in 2022 left many Russian units on unencrypted radios and phones that Ukraine intercepted, a failure widely reported in the first year.

items.name: L3Harris and Motorola radios
items.role: Western encrypted radios in Ukrainian service
items.description: Ukraine's units rely on donated and purchased Western radios, including L3Harris Falcon sets and Motorola handhelds, alongside domestic Ukrainian radios, with Starlink for data. The mixture has made interoperability a persistent problem between brigades.

items.name: Delta and Kropyva
items.role: Battle management software that fuses drone feeds and reports
items.description: Delta is Ukraine's cloud-based situational awareness system, fed by drone video, reports and allied intelligence, adopted across the armed forces in 2023 and made NATO-compatible. Kropyva is the older artillery tablet application used by gun crews. Together they turned reconnaissance into fire missions in minutes.

items.name: Command systems (Russia)
items.role: Automated command and reconnaissance-strike networks
items.description: Russia entered the war with a patchy automated command system and has since built reconnaissance-strike loops around drone video, Telegram-based reporting and dedicated targeting software for Lancet and artillery units. Public detail is thin; assessments describe faster but still centralised targeting.

items.name: Krasukha-4
items.role: Ground-based jammer against radars and satellites
items.description: A truck-mounted broadband jammer meant to blind airborne radars and reconnaissance satellites over hundreds of kilometres. A Krasukha-4 command post was captured intact near Kyiv in March 2022, and the system has appeared in loss lists since.

items.name: R-330Zh Zhitel
items.role: Jammer against satellite navigation and mobile phones
items.description: A mobile jamming station against satellite phones, mobile networks and GNSS receivers, one of the systems behind the dense electronic warfare that forces both sides towards fibre-optic drones and inertial navigation.

items.name: Bukovel-AD and trench jammers
items.role: Anti-drone electronic warfare from vehicle to backpack scale
items.description: Ukraine fields the Bukovel-AD system against reconnaissance drones and a mass of smaller 'trench' jammers fitted to vehicles and carried by infantry to break FPV control links. Their effectiveness fell as both sides moved to new frequencies and fibre-optic control.

items.name: Pole-21
items.role: GNSS jamming network mounted on cell towers
items.description: A jamming system installed on mobile-phone masts to deny GPS, GLONASS and Galileo over wide areas, used to protect Russian cities and rear areas from guided munitions and drones. Its interference is visible in the GPS interference map under the Cyber control.

items.name: Jam-resistant navigation (Ukraine)
items.role: Anti-jam antennas and inertial navigation for drones and munitions
items.description: Ukrainian long-range drones and Western guided munitions increasingly carry controlled reception pattern antennas, inertial units and terrain-matching to fly through jamming. Reported HIMARS and JDAM accuracy problems in 2023 drove the change.

items.name: S-400 Triumf
items.role: Long-range surface-to-air missile system
items.description: Russia's premier long-range air defence system, also used to fire ballistic-trajectory missiles at Ukrainian cities. S-400 batteries in Crimea and occupied territory have been struck repeatedly by ATACMS, Storm Shadow and drones, with radars and launchers documented destroyed.

items.name: S-300V4 and S-300PM
items.role: Army and air-force long-range air defence
items.description: Older long-range systems that remain widespread; the S-300V4 is the army's version with anti-ballistic missiles, and S-300P variants have been fired at ground targets in Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia. Their radars are a favoured target for HIMARS and Ukrainian drones.

items.name: MIM-104 Patriot
items.role: The only Ukrainian system that reliably intercepts ballistic missiles
items.description: Patriot batteries arrived in April 2023 and shot down Kinzhal and Iskander missiles over Kyiv within weeks. They are the backbone of ballistic-missile defence for the capital and other cities, and interceptor supply, not launchers, has been the recurring limit, with each PAC-3 missile costing millions of dollars.
items.numbers: Ukraine has been reported to operate several batteries; exact numbers and interceptor stocks are not public.

items.name: SAMP/T
items.role: European long-range system with Aster missiles
items.description: The Franco-Italian SAMP/T, delivered from 2023, gives Ukraine a second long-range system able to engage ballistic missiles, with Aster 30 interceptors. Missile supply has been limited.

items.name: Buk-M2 and Buk-M3
items.role: Tracked medium-range air defence with the ground forces
items.description: The Buk family provides medium-range cover for Russian ground formations and has been fired at aircraft, HIMARS rockets and drones. Ukraine also fields older Buk-M1s, some adapted to fire Western Sea Sparrow missiles under the FrankenSAM programme.

items.name: NASAMS
items.role: Medium-range system firing AMRAAM missiles
items.description: NASAMS arrived in November 2022 and has been credited with high interception rates against cruise missiles and drones around Kyiv and other cities. It fires the same AMRAAM missiles as Western fighters, which eases supply but competes with F-16 stocks.

items.name: IRIS-T SLM
items.role: German medium-range system, Ukraine was its first user
items.description: Ukraine received the first IRIS-T SLM battery in October 2022, before Germany's own forces, and has reported very high hit rates against cruise missiles and Shaheds. Germany has committed further batteries and short-range SLS launchers.

items.name: MIM-23 Hawk
items.role: Cold War medium-range system returned to service
items.description: Refurbished Hawk batteries from Spain and US stocks gave Ukraine additional medium-range cover from 2023, valued for plentiful missiles against Shahed waves rather than for the newest threats.

items.name: Pantsir-S1
items.role: Gun and missile point defence for bases and cities
items.description: A truck-mounted system with two guns and short-range missiles that guards Russian airfields, the Kremlin and oil facilities against drones. It has been both a frequent Ukrainian target and a frequent claimant of drone kills; footage of Pantsirs on Moscow rooftops became a symbol of the drone campaign.

items.name: Tor-M2
items.role: Tracked short-range system against drones and rockets
items.description: A tracked short-range air defence system moving with Russian brigades, often credited in Russian reporting with shooting down Ukrainian drones and HIMARS rockets, and often found in Ukrainian strike footage.

items.name: Flakpanzer Gepard
items.role: Twin 35 mm anti-aircraft tank, the best Shahed killer per shot
items.description: Retired German anti-aircraft tanks supplied from 2022 became one of Ukraine's most cost-effective defences against Shahed drones, each kill costing a burst of 35 mm shells rather than a missile. Ammunition supply was solved by Rheinmetall restarting production.
items.numbers: Germany and the United States supplied several dozen Gepards.

items.name: Skynex and Skyranger
items.role: Modern 35 mm gun systems with airburst ammunition
items.description: Rheinmetall's Skynex gun system and vehicle-mounted Skyranger turrets bring programmable airburst ammunition against drones, supplied in small numbers from 2023 and 2024 to defend cities and infrastructure.

items.name: Igla and Verba MANPADS
items.role: Shoulder-launched missiles against helicopters and drones
items.description: Russian infantry carries Igla-S and the newer Verba shoulder-launched missiles, which have downed Ukrainian helicopters and attack jets flying low near the line. Both sides also mount MANPADS on vehicles as improvised air defence.

items.name: Stinger, Piorun and mobile fire groups
items.role: MANPADS and pickup-mounted machine guns against drones
items.description: Western shoulder-launched missiles were decisive against Russian helicopters in 2022. Against Shahed waves Ukraine relies on hundreds of mobile fire groups: pickups with heavy machine guns, searchlights and thermal sights that shoot drones down cheaply along their approach routes.

items.name: Counter-drone layers (Ukraine)
items.role: Acoustic sensors, jammers, interceptors and guns in depth
items.description: Ukraine's defence against Shaheds is a layered system: thousands of acoustic sensors that track drones by sound, jammers, interceptor drones, mobile fire groups, gun systems and, as a last resort, missiles. Layering keeps the cost per kill far below the cost of a missile.

items.name: Counter-drone measures (Russia)
items.role: Cage armour, jammers, nets and drone hunters
items.description: Russian vehicles carry welded 'cope cages', anti-drone screens and jammers against FPVs; rear areas rely on Pantsir, helicopters and interceptor drones against Ukraine's long-range types. Netting over roads and 'turtle tank' improvisations show how far the FPV threat has changed the battlefield.

items.name: 9K720 Iskander-M
items.role: Short-range ballistic missile, Russia's most accurate strike weapon
items.description: A road-mobile ballistic missile with a range of about 500 kilometres and a manoeuvring warhead that only Patriot has reliably intercepted. Used throughout the war against cities, command posts and airfields, often paired with the Iskander-K cruise missile from the same launcher.
items.numbers: The General Staff's cumulative claim for missile launchers is shown in the figures above.

items.name: Kh-47M2 Kinzhal
items.role: Air-launched ballistic missile fired from MiG-31s
items.description: An Iskander derivative launched from MiG-31K interceptors, presented by Russia as an unstoppable hypersonic weapon until Patriot crews shot several down over Kyiv in May 2023. It remains among the hardest missiles to intercept.

items.name: KN-23 (North Korean)
items.role: North Korean ballistic missiles supplied to Russia
items.description: From late 2023 Russia fired North Korean KN-23 and KN-24 ballistic missiles at Ukrainian cities, confirmed by debris analysis. Early examples were inaccurate; Ukrainian intelligence later reported improved accuracy as North Korea gained battlefield data.

items.name: Oreshnik
items.role: Intermediate-range ballistic missile first fired at Dnipro in November 2024
items.description: An intermediate-range ballistic missile with multiple warheads, fired at Dnipro on 21 November 2024 in what Russia called a test after Ukraine's first ATACMS strikes on Russian territory. Its inert warheads did limited damage; the launch was a signal rather than a battlefield weapon, and Russia announced deployment to Belarus.

items.name: MGM-140 ATACMS
items.role: HIMARS-launched ballistic missile out to 300 kilometres
items.description: ATACMS arrived secretly in October 2023 and destroyed helicopters at Berdiansk and Luhansk on their first use; the 300-kilometre version followed in 2024 and hit airfields and air defence in Crimea. Permission to fire into Russia came in November 2024 and drew the Oreshnik launch in reply.

items.name: Kh-101 and Kh-555
items.role: Air-launched cruise missiles fired from Tu-95 and Tu-160 bombers
items.description: The main long-range cruise missiles of the strategic bombers, launched from over Russia at power stations and cities in the recurring winter campaigns. Production continued through sanctions with imported electronics, and later missiles added decoys and larger warheads.
items.numbers: The General Staff's cumulative cruise missile claim is shown in the figures above.

items.name: 3M-14 Kalibr
items.role: Ship- and submarine-launched cruise missile from the Black Sea and Caspian
items.description: Fired from Black Sea Fleet corvettes, frigates and Kilo-class submarines, Kalibr salvoes opened many of the mass strikes. Ukrainian naval drones and missile strikes pushed the launch platforms out of Sevastopol and reduced the number of launches from the sea.

items.name: Kh-22 and Kh-32
items.role: Heavy anti-ship missiles fired at cities from Tu-22M3 bombers
items.description: Soviet-era supersonic anti-ship missiles with warheads near a tonne, fired at land targets with poor accuracy; a Kh-22 destroyed the Kremenchuk shopping centre in June 2022 and an apartment block in Dnipro in January 2023. Ukraine had no interceptor for them until Patriot.

items.name: 3M22 Zircon
items.role: Hypersonic cruise missile used in small numbers
items.description: Russia's hypersonic anti-ship cruise missile, fired at Kyiv from early 2024 in small numbers and confirmed from debris. Its speed makes it hard to intercept, but numbers have been low.

items.name: Storm Shadow / SCALP-EG
items.role: Air-launched cruise missile carried by Su-24s
items.description: Supplied from May 2023 and carried by adapted Su-24M bombers, Storm Shadow and its French twin destroyed the Black Sea Fleet headquarters in Sevastopol and a submarine in dry dock. Permission to fire into Russia followed in November 2024.

items.name: R-360 Neptune
items.role: Domestic cruise missile that sank the Moskva, later a land-attack weapon
items.description: Ukraine's anti-ship cruise missile sank the cruiser Moskva in April 2022. A land-attack version with longer range followed and has been used against targets in Crimea and Russia; Ukraine announced a 'Long Neptune' with a range of around 1,000 kilometres in 2025.

items.name: FP-5 Flamingo
items.role: Heavy long-range cruise missile shown in 2025
items.description: A large ground-launched cruise missile from Fire Point, presented in August 2025 with a stated warhead over a tonne and range of about 3,000 kilometres. Ukraine reported its first combat uses against targets in Russia later that year; independent confirmation of numbers is limited.
items.numbers: Fire Point stated a target of several missiles a day; unverified.

items.name: M142 HIMARS and GMLRS
items.role: Guided rocket artillery that changed the war in summer 2022
items.description: HIMARS launchers firing GPS-guided GMLRS rockets to about 80 kilometres arrived in June 2022 and destroyed Russian ammunition depots, bridges and command posts, forcing the withdrawal from Kherson. Russian jamming later degraded accuracy until updated guidance restored it.
items.numbers: The United States and allies supplied several dozen HIMARS and M270 launchers.

items.name: Tornado-S
items.role: Guided 300 mm rocket artillery
items.description: The modernised Smerch with satellite-guided 300 mm rockets, Russia's answer to HIMARS for strikes on airfields and depots at up to 120 kilometres.

items.name: UMPK glide bombs (FAB-500 to FAB-3000)
items.role: Cheap wing kits that turned dumb bombs into stand-off weapons
items.description: From early 2023 Russian Su-34s dropped Soviet-era FAB bombs fitted with folding wings and satellite guidance from outside the range of most Ukrainian air defence, up to a hundred a day by 2024. They levelled defensive positions at Avdiivka and Vuhledar and drove the pressure for F-16s and longer-range air defence.
items.numbers: Ukrainian officials reported several thousand glide bombs a month at the 2024 peak.

items.name: JDAM-ER and GLSDB
items.role: Western glide bombs and ground-launched small diameter bombs
items.description: Ukraine received JDAM-ER guided glide bombs for its MiG-29s and later F-16s, and the ground-launched GLSDB fired from HIMARS. Both suffered from Russian GPS jamming in 2023 and 2024 before updated guidance improved results.

items.name: 2S19 Msta-S
items.role: 152 mm self-propelled howitzer, the backbone of Russian artillery
items.description: Russia's standard tracked 152 mm howitzer, firing conventional and Krasnopol laser-guided shells. Russian artillery fired far more shells than Ukraine through 2022 and 2023, sustained by domestic production and North Korean supply, while losing hundreds of guns to counter-battery fire and Lancets.
items.numbers: The General Staff's cumulative artillery claim is shown in the figures above; Oryx documents around two thousand Russian artillery losses.

items.name: 2S7 Pion and Malka
items.role: 203 mm heavy guns for long-range fire
items.description: Soviet 203 mm guns brought out of storage for the long-range fire that reduced Bakhmut and Avdiivka. Ukraine also fields the 2S7 and once captured a number of them.

items.name: M1989 Koksan (North Korean)
items.role: 170 mm North Korean guns delivered to Russia
items.description: North Korea supplied its 170 mm Koksan self-propelled guns to Russia from late 2024, seen on Russian railways and later on the front, along with millions of shells that helped sustain Russian fire.

items.name: 2S22 Bohdana
items.role: Ukrainian-built 155 mm wheeled howitzer
items.description: Ukraine's own NATO-calibre howitzer, first used at Snake Island in 2022 and produced at a rate reported above twenty a month by 2024 and 2025, making it the most numerous new gun in the army. It fires the same 155 mm ammunition as Western donations.
items.numbers: Ukraine reported production of 20 or more a month in 2024 and 2025.

items.name: CAESAR, PzH 2000, Krab, Archer
items.role: Western 155 mm self-propelled howitzers
items.description: Ukraine's Western self-propelled guns range from the truck-mounted CAESAR and Archer, valued for shoot-and-scoot against counter-battery fire, to the tracked PzH 2000 and Polish Krab. Barrel wear and maintenance have been recurring issues at wartime firing rates.

items.name: M777 howitzer
items.role: Towed 155 mm howitzer, the first Western gun in numbers
items.description: Nearly two hundred M777s arrived in spring 2022 and fired the Excalibur guided shell; their light weight helped mobility but made them vulnerable to Lancets, and many have been damaged and repaired.
items.numbers: Around 190 were supplied in 2022.

items.name: D-30, Msta-B and Giatsint-B
items.role: Towed Soviet-era guns drawn from deep storage
items.description: As self-propelled guns were lost, Russia pulled towed 122 mm and 152 mm guns from Soviet storage sites, visible in satellite counts of shrinking depots. Both sides also use towed guns with the many mobilised units.

items.name: BM-21 Grad and Tornado-G
items.role: 122 mm multiple rocket launchers
items.description: The truck-mounted Grad and its modernised Tornado-G version deliver area fire on Ukrainian positions and towns, the most numerous rocket launchers on both sides. Ukraine fields Grads too, with domestic rockets and Czech RM-70 variants.
items.numbers: The General Staff's cumulative rocket launcher claim is shown in the figures above.

items.name: M270 MLRS and MARS II
items.role: Tracked launchers firing the same GMLRS rockets as HIMARS
items.description: The tracked M270 family from the UK, Germany and France doubled Ukraine's guided rocket capacity in 2022 alongside HIMARS.

items.name: TOS-1A Solntsepyok and TOS-2
items.role: Thermobaric rocket launchers on a tank chassis
items.description: Short-range launchers firing thermobaric rockets that devastate trenches and buildings, used at Mariupol, Bakhmut and Vuhledar. Their short range puts them within reach of drones, and dozens have been documented destroyed.

items.name: AK-12 and AK-74M
items.role: Standard 5.45 mm rifles
items.description: The AK-74M remains the most common Russian rifle, with the newer AK-12 issued from 2018 and revised during the war after complaints about its selector and rail. Mobilised troops have also been seen with older AKMs from storage.

items.name: AK-74, Fort-221 and Western rifles
items.role: A mixed inventory of 5.45 mm and 5.56 mm rifles
items.description: Most Ukrainian infantry still carry the AK-74 in 5.45 mm, with the Israeli-designed Fort-221 in special units and growing numbers of Western 5.56 mm rifles such as the M4, FN SCAR and Czech CZ Bren 2 from donations. The two calibres complicate supply.

items.name: PKM, PKP Pecheneg and Kord
items.role: General-purpose and heavy machine guns
items.description: The 7.62 mm PK family and the 12.7 mm Kord are found in every Russian platoon and on vehicles; the Kord and older NSV serve as improvised anti-drone guns on trucks.

items.name: M240, M2 Browning and Soviet types
items.role: Machine guns including the drone-hunting M2
items.description: Ukraine uses donated M240s and M2 Brownings alongside PKMs and DShKs; the M2 with a thermal sight is the standard weapon of the mobile fire groups that hunt Shahed drones at night.

items.name: Javelin, NLAW and Stugna-P
items.role: The anti-tank weapons that broke the 2022 armoured columns
items.description: Javelin and NLAW became symbols of the defence of Kyiv, and Ukraine's own Stugna-P laser-guided missile has a long record of tank kills. As FPV drones took over the anti-armour role, these weapons became a second layer rather than the first.
items.numbers: The United States announced over 10,000 Javelins by 2023; the UK supplied several thousand NLAWs.

items.name: RPG-7, RPG-30 and Kornet
items.role: Rocket-propelled grenades and the Kornet guided missile
items.description: Russian infantry carries the RPG-7 and disposable RPG-26 and RPG-30 launchers; the Kornet anti-tank missile, also mounted on vehicles, has killed Western tanks including Leopard 2s and Abrams. RPG warheads are also the most common FPV drone payload.

items.name: 2B14 Podnos and 2S12 Sani mortars
items.role: 82 mm and 120 mm mortars
items.description: Mortars provide the closest fire support on both sides; Russia's 82 mm Podnos and 120 mm Sani, and Ukraine's equivalents plus Western 60 mm and 120 mm mortars, fire more rounds daily than most people expect.

items.name: Mk 19 and UAG-40 grenade launchers
items.role: Automatic grenade launchers for trench fighting
items.description: Automatic grenade launchers, American Mk 19s and Ukrainian UAG-40s, sit in Ukrainian defensive positions alongside Soviet AGS-17s; the same 40 mm and 30 mm grenades are dropped from drones.

items.name: T-90M Proryv
items.role: Russia's most modern tank in production
items.description: The T-90M is Russia's best tank in quantity, with new armour, sights and a remote machine gun, and the type Uralvagonzavod concentrates on. Many have been lost, several captured intact by Ukraine, and most now carry improvised cages and screens against drones.
items.numbers: Oryx documents over a hundred T-90M losses; the General Staff's cumulative tank claim is shown in the figures above.

items.name: T-72B3 and T-80BVM
items.role: The most numerous Russian tanks
items.description: Modernised T-72s and gas-turbine T-80s make up the bulk of Russian tank losses and of the tanks still in service. Refurbishment of stored hulls, rather than new production, has sustained the numbers, and satellite counts show storage yards emptying.
items.numbers: Oryx documents several thousand Russian tank losses of all types.

items.name: T-62 and T-55
items.role: Cold War tanks pulled from storage
items.description: From 2022 Russia reactivated T-62s and even T-55s to replace losses, using them as assault guns and fire support with mobilised units. Their appearance became a measure of how deeply reserves were being drawn down.

items.name: T-64BV and T-64BM Bulat
items.role: Ukraine's standard tank, built in Kharkiv
items.description: The T-64 has been Ukraine's main tank since independence, kept running by the Kharkiv plant that built it. Ukraine also fields captured Russian T-72s and T-80s in numbers that at times exceeded its Western deliveries.

items.name: Leopard 2A4, 2A6 and Strv 122
items.role: Western tanks delivered from 2023
items.description: European Leopard 2s arrived for the 2023 counteroffensive and took losses in the minefields of Zaporizhzhia; they remain Ukraine's most capable tanks, with the 2A6 and Swedish Strv 122 the best protected. Spare parts and repair capacity have limited availability.
items.numbers: Around 100 Leopard 2s and 100 older Leopard 1A5s were pledged.

items.name: M1A1 Abrams and Challenger 2
items.role: American and British tanks in small numbers
items.description: The United States supplied 31 M1A1 Abrams and the UK 14 Challenger 2s. Both proved vulnerable to drones and mines in the Avdiivka fighting and were pulled back from the front for a period in 2024; Australia later pledged additional Abrams.
items.numbers: 31 Abrams and 14 Challenger 2s delivered by 2024.

items.name: BMP-3 and BMP-2
items.role: Tracked infantry fighting vehicles
items.description: The BMP-2 is the most common Russian infantry vehicle and the BMP-3 the most modern in production, both losing thin-armoured hulls in large numbers to mines, artillery and FPVs. Losses of infantry vehicles exceed tank losses several times over.
items.numbers: The General Staff's cumulative armoured vehicle claim is shown in the figures above.

items.name: M2A2 Bradley
items.role: Well-armoured American infantry fighting vehicle
items.description: The Bradley became one of Ukraine's most valued vehicles for its protection and its 25 mm gun, with crews surviving hits that would have destroyed a BMP. Losses in the 2023 counteroffensive were often repairable, and a Bradley famously defeated a T-90M near Stepove in January 2024.
items.numbers: More than 300 were supplied by the United States.

items.name: CV90 and Marder 1A3
items.role: European infantry fighting vehicles
items.description: Sweden's CV90 and Germany's Marder gave Ukrainian mechanised brigades modern vehicles from 2023, and Ukraine agreed to produce CV90s domestically. Marders also serve as drone-defence and evacuation vehicles.

items.name: BTR-82A and MT-LB
items.role: Wheeled and tracked armoured personnel carriers
items.description: The BTR-82A wheeled carrier and the MT-LB tractor carry Russian infantry and have been lost by the thousand; the MT-LB has also been fitted with naval guns and rocket pods as improvised fire support, a sign of shortages.

items.name: M113, Stryker and BTR-4
items.role: Armoured personnel carriers including Ukraine's own BTR-4
items.description: Hundreds of M113s from a dozen countries carry Ukrainian infantry and the wounded; Strykers arrived in 2023, and the Ukrainian-built BTR-4 with a 30 mm gun continues in production at Kharkiv.

items.name: MaxxPro, Bushmaster, Kozak and Novator
items.role: Mine-protected vehicles for infantry and evacuation
items.description: Mine-resistant trucks from US and Australian stocks, and Ukrainian-built Kozak and Novator vehicles, carry infantry to the line where tracked vehicles draw too much fire. They are among the most common vehicles in drone footage from both sides.

items.name: Tigr, Typhoon and motorcycles
items.role: Light protected vehicles and, increasingly, unprotected transport
items.description: Russia's Tigr and Typhoon protected vehicles have been joined since 2024 by motorcycles, quad bikes, golf carts and civilian cars for assaults, because drones make any vehicle a target and small numbers of fast riders sometimes get through.

items.name: Su-35S and Su-30SM
items.role: Air-superiority fighters that keep Ukrainian jets back
items.description: Russia's modern fighters patrol from inside Russian airspace with long-range R-37M missiles, denying Ukrainian aircraft the front line. Losses have been modest compared with ground attack types, and Ukraine's Patriot ambushes have caught several near the border.

items.name: F-16 Fighting Falcon
items.role: Ukraine's first Western fighters, flying from August 2024
items.description: European F-16s began operations in August 2024, mostly shooting down cruise missiles and drones and later dropping guided bombs. Pilot training and airfield vulnerability limit their use, and several have been lost, including to friendly fire and Russian missiles.
items.numbers: Around 85 were pledged by four countries.

items.name: Mirage 2000-5F and MiG-29
items.role: French fighters delivered in 2025 beside the Soviet-era fleet
items.description: France delivered Mirage 2000-5Fs in 2025 adapted for air defence and SCALP missiles. Ukraine's MiG-29s and Su-27s, reinforced from Poland and Slovakia, still fly most sorties with HARM anti-radar missiles and glide bombs.

items.name: Su-34
items.role: The bomber that drops most glide bombs
items.description: The Su-34 fighter-bomber carries the UMPK glide bombs that dominate Russian air support. Ukraine has shot down dozens with Patriot ambushes and destroyed others on airfields, but production continues.
items.numbers: Oryx documents several dozen Su-34 losses.

items.name: Su-25 and Su-24M
items.role: Ground-attack jets used at the front
items.description: Russian Su-25s fire unguided rockets in lofted attacks near the line and have suffered heavy losses to MANPADS; Ukraine's own Su-25s and Su-24Ms, the latter adapted to carry Storm Shadow, fly similar profiles.

items.name: Ka-52 and Mi-28
items.role: Attack helicopters with long-range anti-tank missiles
items.description: The Ka-52 was one of Russia's most effective weapons during the 2023 counteroffensive, firing Vikhr missiles from beyond MANPADS range at advancing Ukrainian columns. Ukraine's ATACMS strikes on Berdiansk and Luhansk in October 2023 destroyed a number on the ground.
items.numbers: Oryx documents over 60 Ka-52 losses.

items.name: Mi-8, Mi-24 and Black Hawk
items.role: Transport and attack helicopters
items.description: Ukraine's Mi-8s and Mi-24s fly resupply, evacuation and rocket attacks at low level, with Czech and Slovak donations and a small number of Western Black Hawks used for special operations.

items.name: Tu-95MS, Tu-160 and Tu-22M3
items.role: Strategic bombers that launch the cruise missile waves
items.description: The bombers launch Kh-101, Kh-555 and Kh-22 missiles from deep inside Russia. Ukraine's June 2025 Operation Spiderweb used smuggled FPV drones to hit bombers on airfields as far as Siberia, damaging or destroying a significant share of the small Tu-95 and Tu-22M3 fleets.
items.numbers: Ukraine claimed 41 aircraft hit in Operation Spiderweb; US officials assessed a lower number.

items.name: A-50 airborne early warning
items.role: Radar aircraft, two shot down in early 2024
items.description: Russia's A-50 radar aircraft direct fighters and air defence; Ukraine shot down two in January and February 2024 and damaged another at Machulishchy in Belarus in 2023, leaving Russia with a handful.

items.name: Black Sea Fleet surface ships
items.role: Frigates, corvettes and landing ships, many lost or withdrawn
items.description: The fleet lost its flagship Moskva in April 2022 and then landing ships, a submarine and patrol ships to missiles and naval drones, before withdrawing most vessels from Sevastopol to Novorossiysk in late 2023. Its remaining corvettes still launch Kalibr missiles from the eastern Black Sea.
items.numbers: Ukraine claims around a third of the fleet destroyed or disabled; Oryx documents over 20 vessels lost or damaged.

items.name: Improved Kilo-class submarines
items.role: Diesel submarines that launch Kalibr missiles
items.description: Six Improved Kilo submarines of the Black Sea Fleet launch Kalibr cruise missiles; one, Rostov-on-Don, was destroyed in dry dock by Storm Shadow in September 2023 and again after repair in August 2024.

items.name: Ukrainian Navy: Neptune batteries, patrol boats and marines
items.role: A navy without large ships that dominates the western Black Sea
items.description: Ukraine scuttled its flagship in 2022 and fights at sea with coastal Neptune missiles, naval drones, small patrol boats from the United States and Europe and marine brigades that hold the Dnipro's islands and banks. It reopened the grain corridor without a single warship.

items.name: AN/TPQ-36 and AN/TPQ-37 Firefinder
items.role: Counter-battery radar
items.description: Among the first Western systems handed over in 2022. The radar watches the sky above the front, catches shells and mortar bombs in flight and runs the trajectory back to the gun that fired them, so artillery or a drone can answer within minutes. Radars radiate, and radiating is dangerous: crews shoot and move, because Lancet drones and anti-radiation missiles hunt them.
items.numbers: United States drawdown fact sheets have listed counter-artillery and counter-mortar radars among the packages since 2022; no running total by type is published.

items.name: AN/TPQ-53
items.role: Counter-fire radar that also tracks drones
items.description: A newer electronically scanned counter-fire radar supplied from 2022. It finds guns, mortars and rockets and can be switched to an air surveillance mode that picks up aircraft and drones, which matters on a front where the two problems are the same problem.

items.name: ARTHUR and COBRA
items.origin: Sweden, Germany, France and the United Kingdom
items.role: European counter-battery radars
items.description: Two European counter-battery radars given to Ukraine: the Swedish ARTHUR, carried on a truck and quick to move, and the larger COBRA phased-array radar, which Germany lists among its deliveries. Both do the same job as the Firefinders and are just as much of a target once they radiate.

items.name: 1L220UK Zoopark-3
items.role: Ukrainian counter-battery radar
items.description: Ukraine's own counter-battery radar, developed before the full-scale invasion from the Soviet Zoopark family and built in small numbers. Domestic production matters because donated radars are finite and losses are steady.

items.name: 1L260 Zoopark-1M
items.role: Counter-battery radar
items.description: Russia's standard counter-battery radar, mounted on a tracked chassis. It has been one of the most sought-after targets for Ukrainian HIMARS and drone crews since 2022: each one destroyed blinds a sector's artillery duel for a while.
items.numbers: Oryx has documented dozens of destroyed or damaged Zoopark-1M radars since 2022; visually confirmed losses are an undercount by design.

items.name: 1L271 Aistenok
items.role: Portable counter-mortar and ground surveillance radar
items.description: A small radar carried by a crew rather than a vehicle. It finds mortars, corrects friendly mortar fire and can watch a stretch of ground for moving vehicles, which makes it the battalion-level counterpart to Zoopark.

items.name: SNAR-10 and Credo-1E ground surveillance radars
items.role: Battlefield surveillance radars
items.description: Radars that look along the ground rather than up: the tracked SNAR-10 Leopard and the portable Credo family detect vehicles and moving groups out to tens of kilometres and hand the coordinates to artillery. Thermal drones have taken over much of this work, but radar keeps working in weather that grounds drones.

items.name: Nebo-U and Nebo-M
items.role: Long-range surveillance radars
items.description: The metre-wave and multiband radars that give Russian air defence its early picture and are meant to see aircraft designed to be hard to see. Several Nebo components have been destroyed in Crimea by ATACMS strikes and drones, which is one reason Russian air defence coverage over the peninsula has gaps.

items.name: Podlet-K1 and Kasta-2E2
items.role: Low-altitude air surveillance radars
items.description: Radars built to see what long-range sets miss: cruise missiles, drones and helicopters flying low. They cue S-400 and Pantsir batteries, and they have been priority targets for Ukrainian strikes on Crimea since 2023.

items.name: 36D6 and P-18 radars
items.role: Legacy air surveillance radars
items.description: Soviet-designed radars, some built in Ukraine, that still feed the national air picture alongside Western sets. They are old, but they are numerous, mobile and cheap enough to risk; crews move them constantly because Russian anti-radiation missiles listen for them.

items.name: AN/MPQ-64 Sentinel and donated air defence radars
items.role: Fire control and surveillance radars for Western systems
items.description: Each donated air defence system brings its own radar: Sentinel sets arrive with NASAMS, IRIS-T and Patriot have theirs. Ukraine has spent the war stitching these into one picture with its Soviet radars so that a battery anywhere can be told what is coming.

items.name: Sky Fortress acoustic sensor network
items.role: Acoustic detection of drones and cruise missiles
items.description: Thousands of cheap microphone posts on poles across the country, listening for the engine note of a Shahed-type drone and passing a track to the mobile fire groups that shoot them down. Ukrainian officials and allied air force officers have described it publicly as one of the cheapest useful things in the air defence system; the detail of coverage is not published.

items.name: 1B75 Penicillin
items.role: Acoustic and thermal counter-battery complex
items.description: Locates guns by the sound of the shot and the heat of the muzzle flash rather than by radar, so it gives nothing away to anti-radiation missiles. Reported in service in small numbers from 2020 and used alongside Zoopark radars.

items.name: Thermal imagers and night sights (Ukraine)
items.role: Night vision, thermal sights and clip-on imagers
items.description: Donated monoculars, weapon sights and clip-on thermal imagers, plus Ukrainian-made imagers, bought at scale by volunteer foundations as well as the state. Thermal imaging decides night fighting: it finds the crew that moved, and it is what a drone operator looks through after dark.

items.name: Night and thermal sights (Russia)
items.role: Night vision and thermal sights
items.description: Russian 1PN-series sights and night vision goggles, heavily supplemented since 2022 by imported Chinese thermal imagers and hunting optics bought commercially. Sanctions reporting and customs analysis have traced much of this trade, which is legal in China and hard to stop.

items.name: ICEYE radar satellites
items.role: Synthetic aperture radar imagery
items.description: Ukraine gained access to ICEYE's radar satellites in 2022 through a purchase funded by the Serhiy Prytula Foundation with money raised from the public. Radar imagery works through cloud and at night, which optical satellites cannot do, and it is used to watch airfields, bridges and troop concentrations.

items.name: Commercial imagery and allied intelligence sharing
items.role: Optical satellite imagery and shared intelligence
items.description: Imagery from Maxar, Planet and Airbus, bought or donated through allied contracts, sits behind much of Ukraine's targeting and behind most open-source analysis of the war. It is a dependency as well as an asset: interruptions to American intelligence sharing in 2025 were reported to degrade Ukrainian targeting within days.

items.name: Persona, Bars-M and Kondor-FKM satellites
items.role: Military reconnaissance satellites
items.description: Russia's optical and radar reconnaissance constellation is small by Western standards and ageing, which is one reason Russian targeting leans so heavily on drones. Launches of Bars-M optical and Kondor-FKM radar satellites have continued through the war.

items.name: Reported Chinese commercial imagery support
items.search: China and the Russian invasion of Ukraine
items.role: Alleged commercial satellite imagery supplied to Russian forces
items.description: Ukrainian military intelligence and United States officials have said Chinese commercial satellite firms provided imagery used for Russian strikes, and the European Union has sanctioned firms on that basis. Beijing denies it. This entry records an allegation by interested parties, not an established fact.

links.label: Wikipedia: China and the Russo-Ukrainian war

items.name: PMP and PP-2005M pontoon parks
items.role: River crossing equipment
items.description: Truck-carried pontoon sections that unfold into a floating bridge. The failed crossing of the Siverskyi Donets near Bilohorivka in May 2022, where Ukrainian artillery caught a Russian force on and around a pontoon bridge, destroyed most of a battalion tactical group's vehicles and became the standing illustration of how hard opposed crossings are under drone observation.

items.name: MTU-72 and TMM-6 bridgelayers
items.role: Assault and gap-crossing bridges
items.description: Armoured bridgelayers that drop a span across a ditch or stream for an assault, and truck-mounted TMM sets that build a longer bridge behind the line. Ukrainian defences dig anti-tank ditches precisely to force their use, and drones wait for them.

items.name: Biber bridgelayers and Dachs engineer vehicles
items.role: Armoured bridging and engineer support
items.description: German-supplied Biber bridgelayers put a span over a gap under fire, and Dachs armoured engineer vehicles dig, clear and recover with a crew under armour. Both appear on the German government's published list of deliveries to Ukraine.

items.name: The Surovikin line
items.role: Prepared defensive belts and obstacles
items.description: The belts of anti-tank ditches, dragon's teeth, trenches and dense minefields dug across Zaporizhzhia and Kherson from late 2022, named in reporting after General Sergei Surovikin. Together with helicopters and drones they stopped Ukraine's 2023 counter-offensive in the first belt, and they are the clearest evidence that Russia learned to prepare ground.

items.name: The 2024 fortification programme
items.role: State-funded defensive lines
items.description: After criticism that positions behind the front were not prepared, Ukraine funded a national fortification programme in 2024 for Donetsk, Kharkiv and Sumy. Ukrainian audits, journalists and soldiers have reported delays, positions built too far back or in the wrong places, and procurement scandals alongside the lines that were built.

items.name: ISDM Zemledeliye
items.role: Remote mining system
items.description: A rocket launcher that lays a minefield instead of firing explosives at a target: it can seed mines across a road, a crossing site or the ground behind an advancing unit within minutes. It turns mining from an engineering task into an artillery one.

items.name: PFM-1 Lepestok and POM-3 mines
items.role: Scatterable anti-personnel mines
items.description: The PFM-1 petal mine, small, green and shaped like a leaf, was scattered into Izium and other occupied towns; Human Rights Watch documented its use in inhabited areas. The POM-3 uses a seismic sensor to detect a walking person and jumps before exploding. Both are banned for Ukraine under the Ottawa Convention, which Russia never joined.

items.name: RAAM artillery-delivered mines
items.role: Remote anti-armour mining
items.description: 155mm shells that scatter anti-tank mines, used to close a gap in front of an armoured assault without sending engineers forward. The United States also approved the transfer of anti-personnel mines in late 2024, a decision criticised by campaigners because Ukraine is a party to the Ottawa Convention and later moved to withdraw from it.

items.name: UR-77 Meteorit
items.role: Mine-clearing line charge vehicle
items.description: Fires a rocket that drags an explosive hose across a minefield and detonates it, blasting a lane. In this war it has been used at least as often to demolish buildings in urban assaults, a practice recorded repeatedly in Russian footage from Bakhmut and elsewhere.

items.name: Uran-6 and IMR-3M
items.role: Demining robot and armoured engineer vehicle
items.description: The small tracked Uran-6 flails ground ahead of troops by remote control; the IMR-3M is a tank-based engineer vehicle with a dozer blade and a crane that clears rubble and obstacles under armour. Both predate the war and both are scarce relative to the frontage.

items.name: M58 MICLIC, ploughs and rollers
items.role: Breaching equipment for assault lanes
items.description: Line charges fired across a minefield, and ploughs and rollers bolted to the front of tanks. Shortages of this unglamorous equipment, and of the training to use it under fire, were among the reasons the 2023 counter-offensive stalled in the first Russian minefield belt.

items.name: Bozena, MV-4 and Armtrac demining machines
items.origin: Slovakia, Croatia and the United Kingdom
items.role: Route and humanitarian demining
items.description: Remote-controlled flail and tiller machines donated for clearing roads, fields and returned territory. The scale is the problem: Ukrainian and United Nations statements describe one of the most heavily mined countries in the world and a clearance task measured in decades and billions of dollars.

items.name: KamAZ Mustang and Ural trucks
items.role: Military cargo trucks
items.description: The trucks that carry Russian shells, fuel and food. Early in the war their loss to ambushes exposed how thin Russian logistics were; now the threat is FPV and bomber drones watching every approach road, which has pushed supply runs to night, to dispersal and to smaller vehicles.

items.name: Motorcycles, quad bikes and Desertcross buggies
items.role: Light assault and resupply transport
items.description: From 2024 Russian units increasingly attacked and resupplied on motorcycles, quad bikes and Chinese Desertcross 1000-3 buggies, because armoured vehicles are found and killed by drones before they arrive. It is cheap, fast and appalling for the rider: Ukrainian and Russian footage of motorcycle assaults is abundant.

items.name: Donated trucks and tank transporters
items.role: Cargo, fuel and heavy equipment transport
items.description: FMTV and HEMTT military trucks, European commercial lorries and heavy equipment transporters that move tanks to and from repair. Sustaining donated Western vehicles requires this fleet as much as the vehicles themselves, and it is rarely counted in headline aid figures.

items.name: Pickups and volunteer vehicles
items.origin: Japan, Europe and the United States (donated)
items.role: Last-mile transport for drone crews and ammunition
items.description: Second-hand pickups, vans and 4x4s bought by volunteer foundations and driven to the front, where they move drone teams, batteries, water and wounded over the last few kilometres. Losses to FPV drones are heavy and constant, and replacing them is a permanent fundraising campaign.

items.name: Sea mines in the Black Sea
items.role: Moored and drifting sea mines
items.description: Mines laid in the north-western Black Sea from 2022 closed shipping lanes and threatened the grain corridor. Drifting mines washed up on the Turkish, Romanian and Bulgarian coasts and were destroyed by national navies; Turkey, Romania and Bulgaria set up a joint mine countermeasures group in 2024. Each side blames the other for the drifting mines, and attribution of individual mines is rarely possible.

items.name: Ukrainian coastal minefields
items.search: Blockade of the Gulf of Odesa
items.role: Defensive mining of the approaches to Odesa
items.description: Ukraine mined the approaches to Odesa and the Dnipro-Buh estuary in 2022 against an amphibious landing that never came. The minefields also helped close Ukraine's own ports until the grain corridor arrangements, and clearing them is a condition of normal shipping returning.

items.name: K-300P Bastion-P and Bal
items.role: Coastal anti-ship missile systems
items.description: Mobile launchers in Crimea and Krasnodar carrying Oniks and Kh-35 missiles. They are anti-ship systems used mostly against land targets in this war, including strikes on Odesa, and they have been hit repeatedly by ATACMS and naval drones because their positions are known.

items.name: Murmansk-BN
items.role: Long-range shortwave jamming complex
items.description: A truck-mounted complex with masts tens of metres high that jams high-frequency radio over very long distances, claimed by its maker to reach thousands of kilometres. It is deployed in Crimea and Kaliningrad and is aimed at long-haul military communications rather than at anything on the front line.

items.name: Shipovnik-Aero
items.role: Counter-drone electronic warfare vehicle
items.description: A vehicle-mounted system for finding, jamming and spoofing drone control and video links, credited by Russian sources with taking over drones in flight. Captured examples have been examined by Ukrainian specialists, and it is one of the systems Ukrainian crews try to locate and strike first.

items.name: Silok and Repellent-1
items.role: Point counter-drone jammers
items.description: Jammers built to protect a headquarters, an airfield or a depot rather than a unit in contact: they sweep the control and navigation bands used by small drones. Their effectiveness against fibre-optic drones, which carry no radio link at all, is nil.

items.name: Nota and Ai-Petri electronic warfare complexes
items.search: Electronic warfare in the Russo-Ukrainian War
items.role: Ukrainian jamming and direction finding
items.description: Domestically built complexes for jamming Russian communications and drone links and for direction finding. Ukrainian production scaled up sharply from 2023 because donated electronic warfare equipment arrived slowly and the drone problem grew faster.

items.name: Trench and vehicle counter-drone jammers
items.role: Squad and vehicle protection against FPV drones
items.description: Backpack and roof-mounted jammer domes, many from Ukrainian makers such as Kvertus, that put a bubble of interference around a dugout or a pickup. They work against radio-guided FPV drones, interfere with friendly radios and navigation, and do nothing against fibre-optic drones.

items.name: Tobol satellite interference complexes
items.role: Interference with satellite navigation and satellite links
items.description: Fixed complexes reported by Western media, on the basis of leaked United States assessments, to be used against satellite navigation and satellite communications including Starlink. Russia describes Tobol as a system for protecting its own satellites. Public evidence is limited and the entry reflects reporting rather than confirmation.

items.name: Pokrova
items.role: National satellite navigation spoofing system
items.description: A Ukrainian system announced by officials in 2024 that broadcasts false satellite navigation signals to push Shahed-type drones and guided bombs off course over a wide area. Its effect is disputed, it degrades civilian navigation across the same airspace, and independent assessment is not possible from public sources.

items.name: Himera G1 radios
items.role: Jam-resistant tactical handheld radios
items.description: Ukrainian frequency-hopping handhelds designed after 2022 for a jammed battlefield and priced so that a company can be issued them rather than a headquarters. Encrypted Western radios remain scarce, so cheap domestic radios matter more than they should.

items.name: R-168 Akveduk and civilian handhelds
items.role: Tactical radios and unencrypted commercial sets
items.description: The R-168 family is the Russian army's standard tactical radio, but shortages and unfamiliarity pushed units onto unencrypted commercial handhelds bought on the civilian market. Ukrainian electronic warfare and volunteer intercept groups have harvested Russian traffic from these radios throughout the war.

items.name: Strelets reconnaissance and control sets
items.role: Target data from scouts to artillery
items.description: A soldier-carried set that passes coordinates, images and orders between reconnaissance teams, commanders and artillery or Iskander batteries. It is the Russian answer to the problem Ukraine solved with Kropyva and Delta, and it is the link that makes a spotted target into a strike.

items.name: S-350 Vityaz
items.role: Medium-range surface-to-air system
items.description: A newer medium-range system carrying many 9M96 missiles per launcher, intended to relieve S-400 batteries of drone and cruise missile work. Fielded from 2019 and reported in combat use in this war; several launchers have been claimed destroyed by Ukrainian strikes.

items.name: FrankenSAM hybrids
items.role: Western missiles fired from Soviet launchers
items.description: Improvised systems that marry Western missiles to Soviet launchers and radars, the best known firing RIM-7 Sea Sparrow missiles from a Buk launcher. They exist because Ukraine has Soviet launchers and no Soviet missiles left to fire from them, and because Western launchers are scarce.

items.name: Su-24M and Su-25
items.role: Strike and close air support aircraft
items.description: The Su-24M is the aircraft that carries Storm Shadow and SCALP-EG cruise missiles, modified in Ukraine to do so; the Su-25 flies lofted rocket attacks at treetop height because anything higher is inside Russian air defence. Both types are Soviet-built, irreplaceable and steadily lost.

items.name: Saab ASC 890
items.role: Airborne early warning and control aircraft
items.description: Sweden announced the donation of two ASC 890 radar aircraft in 2024. They give Ukraine its own airborne radar picture at altitude, which matters for the F-16 force and for seeing low-flying missiles and drones earlier than ground radar can.

items.name: 2S1 Gvozdika, 2S3 Akatsiya and 2S5
items.role: Soviet self-propelled howitzers
items.description: The Soviet-designed guns that still make up a large part of Ukraine's artillery park, kept firing by donated Polish, Bulgarian, Czech and Greek stocks and by Ukrainian overhaul plants. They are less accurate and shorter-ranged than the Western guns that get the attention, and there are many more of them.

items.name: FH70, L119 and Soviet towed guns
items.role: Towed howitzers of mixed calibre
items.description: Italian and British FH70 and L119 guns, American M101s and Soviet D-20, D-30 and 2A65 pieces, all in service at once. Mixed calibres and mixed ammunition are a logistic burden Ukraine accepted in 2022 because guns were guns.

items.name: BM-27 Uragan and BM-30 Smerch
items.role: Heavy rocket artillery
items.description: Larger and longer-ranged than the Grad, and frequently fired with cluster warheads. Both types have been documented by human rights organisations in strikes on residential areas, where an unguided salvo over a city block is indiscriminate by nature.

items.name: RPO-A Shmel
items.role: Infantry thermobaric rocket launcher
items.description: A shoulder-fired tube whose rocket carries a thermobaric mixture, used against buildings, dugouts and trench positions. It puts the effect of a small artillery shell in the hands of an assault group, and its use in built-up areas has been widely recorded.

items.name: AGM-88 HARM
items.role: Anti-radiation missile
items.description: Supplied in 2022 and improvised onto Soviet MiG-29 and Su-27 aircraft, a modification American engineers and Ukrainian crews worked out together and one of the more surprising technical results of the war. The missile homes on radar emissions, which forces Russian air defence radars to stay quiet or move.

items.name: Kh-31P and Kh-35
items.role: Anti-radiation and anti-ship missiles
items.description: The Kh-31P hunts radars, which is why Ukrainian air defence crews move their sets after every engagement; the Kh-35 is an anti-ship missile regularly fired at land targets from coastal launchers and aircraft.

items.name: Kh-59MK2 and Kh-69
items.role: Air-launched stealthy cruise missiles
items.description: Smaller and harder to detect than the Kh-101, fired from tactical aircraft rather than bombers. Ukrainian officials and analysts identified the Kh-69 in the strike that destroyed the Trypilska power station in April 2024, a case that showed how thin air defence coverage of the grid had become.

items.name: Hrim-2 (Sapsan)
items.role: Ukrainian short-range ballistic missile
items.description: A Ukrainian ballistic missile programme begun before the full-scale invasion and revived during it. Ukrainian officials said in 2025 that it had been used against targets in Russia and was entering serial production. Those are the manufacturer's and government's claims; independent confirmation of numbers or performance is not available.

items.name: Snipex Alligator and T-Rex
items.role: 14.5mm anti-materiel rifles
items.description: Ukrainian-built rifles firing the heavy 14.5mm round designed for anti-tank rifles, used against observation posts, light vehicles, antennas and parked drones at long range. They are heavy, loud and distinctly Ukrainian: a domestic industry that did not exist at this scale before 2014.

items.name: Barrett M107 and Accuracy International rifles
items.role: Donated precision and anti-materiel rifles
items.description: Western .50 calibre and .338 rifles donated from 2022. A Ukrainian security service sniper claimed a record shot of about 3,800 metres in 2023 with a Ukrainian-built rifle; the claim rests on the service's own footage and has not been independently verified.

items.name: SVD, SVDM and Chukavin SVCh
items.role: Marksman and sniper rifles
items.description: The SVD is the marksman's rifle in every Russian platoon and is older than most of the soldiers carrying it; the SVCh is its intended replacement, seen in small numbers. Ordinary infantry marksmanship matters less in a war decided by drones and artillery, but trench lines are still close enough for it.

items.name: ASVK Kord and Orsis T-5000
items.role: Anti-materiel and precision rifles
items.description: The 12.7mm ASVK is Russia's heavy anti-materiel rifle; the commercial Orsis T-5000 is used by special units and was bought in numbers by volunteers. Both appear in Russian sniper publicity, which is a poor guide to how much they matter.

items.name: BMP-1, BMP-2 and BMP-1TS
items.role: Soviet infantry fighting vehicles
items.description: Still the most numerous Ukrainian infantry fighting vehicles, topped up by Czech, Polish and Greek donations and by Ukrainian rebuilds such as the BMP-1TS with a modern turret. Thin armour, a 1960s design and a high casualty rate: crews use them as battle taxis that stop short of the objective.

items.name: BMD-2, BMD-4M and BTR-D
items.role: Airborne infantry fighting vehicles
items.description: Light, air-droppable vehicles built for the airborne forces, with armour thin enough to be opened by heavy machine gun fire. The VDV has fought as ordinary infantry since 2022 and lost these vehicles in quantity doing work they were never designed for.

items.name: Leopard 1A5
items.role: Legacy main battle tank
items.description: A 1970s tank with modern fire control, donated in quantity from 2023 after Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands bought back stored vehicles. Its armour is inadequate against modern anti-tank weapons, so Ukrainian crews use it as a mobile gun firing from cover rather than as an assault tank.
